To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
salt stress inhibits the electron transport at donor and acceptor side of PSII, resulting in damage to phcyobilisome, which leads to the shift of excitation energy distribution in favour of PSI.
salinity stress induced an inhibition of PSII electron transfer at both donor and the acceptor sides of the PSII reaction center.
salinity stress induced a decline in PSII photochemical efficiency and a shift in the distribution of excited energy in favour of the PSI reaction centre.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of salt stress on PSII function in cyanobacteria.
the effects of salinity stress (from 0 to 0.8M NaCl) on the photosystem II (PSII) electron transport in the cyanobacterium Spirulina platenses cells.
the changes in PSII function in Spirulina cells exposed to salinities ranging from 0 to 0.8M NaCl.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
salt stress induced damage to the photosynthetic apparatus of S. platensis cells.
salt stress induced a decrease of the quantum yield of oxygen evolution and PSII photochemistry, and resulted in damage to the photosystem and phycobilisomes in Spirulina cells.
the effects of salinity stress in Spirulina were similar to those of the effects of DCMUI in the control cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the salt stress induced damage to PSII and phycobilisomes, which in turn led to the decrease in PSII photochemical efficiency.
salinity stress inhibited PSII function by affecting the electron transport at the donor and acceptor side of PSII and by damaging the phycobilisomes.

salt stress caused a significant inhibition of the electron transport in PSII and the damage to the PSII reaction centre was more pronounced in salt-stressed than that in the DCMU-treated control cells.

the effects of salinity stress were more pronounced in PSII than PSI.
